title: Sodium in air decides whether hydrogen flames glow orange or vanish

slides.headline: A hydrogen flame can nearly vanish. Salt decides.

caption:
Natural gas burns blue, and anyone can see it. Hydrogen is not so simple.

Researchers at Adelaide University in Australia, working with the University of New South Wales and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia, have found that a hydrogen flame can look very different from one day to the next, even when the burner is set exactly the same way. Sometimes it glows bright orange. Sometimes it is almost invisible.

The reason is sodium in the air. Tiny airborne particles carry it, and sea salt blown inland by wind is one important source. Sodium makes flames glow orange, the same effect used in school flame tests. In two weeks of outdoor testing around Adelaide, the sodium light signal changed by more than 28 times. Air that had passed over the ocean generally gave stronger orange flames.

On average, hydrogen flames also gave off less visible light than natural gas flames. Hydrogen can make faint blue and red light, but that is easy to spot only in a darkened room.

That matters for safety. If you cannot trust your eyes to tell a hydrogen burner is lit, a stove or oven needs other ways to know, such as ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors. The authors say this does not undermine hydrogen's promise. Appliances just have to be designed for its quirks.

Source: Next Energy journal via ScienceDaily
